fixes.explanation: The text says it plainly: “…the earth was illuminated by his glory.” This angel comes down from heaven with great authority. I flip on the kitchen light before sunrise and feel pretty important. This angel makes my light switch look like a birthday candle.

That's the news, and he says it twice: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” The angel cries it out in a mighty voice. Then he says what she has become: a lair for demons and a haunt for every unclean spirit. I'd say that's a message with some volume behind it.
The angel says the opposite. The merchants “…have grown wealthy from the extravagance of her luxury.” Her luxury was making them richer, not poorer. Poor isn't in the verse.
That's it. The voice says to come out “…so that you will not share in her sins or contract any of her plagues.” Coming out is how they avoid both. That's the warning, plain and simple.
She says nothing like that. In her heart she says, “I sit as queen; I am not a widow and will never see grief.” Fear isn't in her words. She's talking about never seeing grief.
The voice doesn't describe a slow stretch of time. It says, “…her plagues will come in one day…” That's the opposite of many generations. One day is the answer.

That's what the text says: the kings “…will weep and wail at the sight of the smoke rising from the fire that consumes her.” They lived in luxury with her. Now they watch the smoke and weep. I think this one is heavy.

The kings aren't cheering. They “…will weep and wail at the sight of the smoke rising from the fire that consumes her.” Later in the passage, heaven and the saints and apostles and prophets are told to rejoice. These kings weep.

The text doesn't show the kings rushing in. They “…will weep and wail…” at the sight of the smoke. Then they stand at a distance and cry out, “Woe, woe to the great city…” Rushing in isn't part of the picture.
That's it. The kings “…will stand at a distance…” in fear of her torment. They watch from far off. Then they cry out, “Woe, woe to the great city, the mighty city of Babylon!”

That's the reason in the text: “…because there is no one left to buy their cargo…” The merchants weep and mourn over her. Gold, silver, pearls, fine linen and more are on their list. Without a buyer, none of it moves.
The kings aren't mentioned in that reason. The merchants weep and mourn “…because there is no one left to buy their cargo…” The text says nothing about a bill. Their reason is no buyer.

That's what they say. The merchants cry, “Woe, woe to the great city, clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls!” It's a picture of her at her fanciest. That's the picture they paint in their cry.
That's their cry. At the sight of the smoke, they exclaim, “What city was ever like this great city?” They're looking back at how great she was. I think they're still in shock.

That's the word. They cry, “…where all who had ships on the sea were enriched by her wealth!” Everyone who had ships on the sea was enriched by her wealth. Then they cry that in a single hour she has been destroyed.
Frightened isn't the word in this line. They cry, “…where all who had ships on the sea were enriched by her wealth!” Enriched means they got richer from her wealth. That's the word the text uses.

That's right. The merchants “…will stand at a distance, in fear of her torment.” (verse 15). The shipmasters, passengers and sailors “…will stand at a distance…” too (verse 17). The kings do the same (verse 10).

That's the call: “Rejoice over her, O heaven, and you saints and apostles and prophets…” The kings, merchants and sailors mourn her. Heaven and the saints and apostles and prophets get a different message. They're told to rejoice.

Mercy isn't the word in this verse. It says, “…because God has pronounced for you His judgment against her.” That's the reason heaven and the saints and apostles and prophets are told to rejoice. The word is judgment.

No breaking in the text. The mighty angel picked up the stone and “…cast it into the sea…” He throws it, and then he says what it stands for. I couldn't even lift a stone that size, so I'm glad this wasn't my job.
The angel says the opposite. “Nor will any craftsmen of any trade be found in you again…” No craftsmen of any trade will be found in her. That covers any trade at all.
No army in this line. The angel says, “…the voices of a bride and bridegroom will never call out in you again.” It's a happy sound. The voices of a bride and bridegroom.
That's the word: “…because all the nations were deceived by your sorcery.” The nations were deceived by her sorcery. That's what the angel says.
Healed isn't what the verse says. It reads, “…because all the nations were deceived by your sorcery.” The nations were deceived by her sorcery. Deceived is the word.
Blessed isn't the word in this verse. The angel says, “…because all the nations were deceived by your sorcery.” The nations were deceived by her sorcery. Deceived is the word the text uses.
